idiom_name: Pundit policy classes invoked from the controller (authorize / policy_scope)
implementation_notes: Pundit keeps the decision in plain Ruby policy classes - PostPolicy#update? receives current_user and the record - and the enforcement in the controller: authorize @post infers the policy class and the query method from the action and raises Pundit::NotAuthorizedError, which the application maps to 403; collections go through policy_scope(Post) so the returned rows are already the permitted ones. Because authorize is explicit, wire the verification hooks (verify_authorized / verify_policy_scoped, or raise_on_missing_policy) so an action that forgets it fails loudly. CanCanCan's central Ability#authorize! with load_and_authorize_resource is the equivalent realization; in both cases the controller never evaluates rules inline.
code_sketch:
class OrdersController < ApplicationController
  include Pundit::Authorization
  before_action :set_order, only: %i[show update]
  after_action :verify_authorized, except: :index

  def update
    authorize @order                       # decision: OrderPolicy#update?
    @order.update!(order_params)
  end

  private
  def set_order = @order = policy_scope(Order).find(params[:id])   # scoped lookup
end
pitfalls: authorize is not automatic: an action that forgets it is unprotected, so enable the verify_authorized/raise_on_missing_policy hooks instead of trusting review.
Rescuing Pundit::NotAuthorizedError into a redirect or a generic error without a 403 hides the decision and can mask a broken policy.
Policies that query the database per attribute or call other policies make the decision slow and order-dependent; one policy stays responsible for one record type.
